## Managing uv

Let's start by checking that `uv` is installed.
Two checks work for any command-line program.
`which` tells you *where* the program is,
and `--version` confirms that it actually runs.

::: {.panel-tabset group="shell"}
## macOS and Linux

```bash
which uv
```

## Windows (Git Bash)

```bash
which uv
```

## Windows (PowerShell)

```powershell
where.exe uv
```
:::

```out
/opt/homebrew/bin/uv
```

```bash
uv --version
```

```out
uv 0.13.7 (Homebrew 2026-11-03 aarch64-apple-darwin)
```

If you get a `command not found` message,
install `uv` by following its
[installation guide](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/).

To see which `uv` commands are available,
type `uv --help`.
To see the full documentation for any of these commands,
type the command followed by `--help`.
For example,
to learn about the `uv add` command:

```bash
uv add --help
```

```bash
uv --help
```

```out
An extremely fast Python package manager.

Usage: uv [OPTIONS] <COMMAND>

Commands:
  auth       Manage authentication
  run        Run a command or script
  init       Create a new project
  add        Add dependencies to the project
  remove     Remove dependencies from the project
  version    Read or update the project's version
  sync       Update the project's environment
  lock       Update the project's lockfile
  export     Export the project's lockfile to an alternate format
  tree       Display the project's dependency tree
  format     Format Python code in the project
  check      Run checks on the project
  audit      Audit the project's dependencies
  tool       Run and install commands provided by Python packages
  python     Manage Python versions and installations
  pip        Manage Python packages with a pip-compatible interface
  venv       Create a virtual environment
  build      Build Python packages into source distributions and wheels
  publish    Upload distributions to an index
  workspace  Inspect uv workspaces
  cache      Manage uv's cache
  self       Manage the uv executable
  help       Display documentation for a command
```

That list is worth reading once.
The commands near the top of the list
(`run`, `init`, `add`, `remove`, `sync`, `lock`)
are the ones you will use every day,
and they are the ones the uv chapters cover.

### Updating uv

If you installed `uv` with the standalone installer,
it can update itself:

```bash
uv self update
```

If you installed it through a package manager,
`uv` will tell you so and hand you the right command instead:

```bash
uv self update
```

```out
error: uv was installed through an external package manager and cannot update itself.

hint: You installed uv using Homebrew. To update uv, run `brew update && brew upgrade uv`
```

This is a nice example of a program giving you an error message
that also tells you how to fix it.
Read your error messages.

## Managing Python versions

One of the jobs `uv` takes over is installing Python itself.
You do not need to download Python from python.org
or install it through Homebrew first.

To see the Python versions `uv` knows about
(both the ones already on your machine and the ones it could download):

```bash
uv python list
```

The output is longer than you expect,
and it is important to understand what it is *not*:

```out
cpython-3.16.0a1-macos-aarch64-none                 <download available>
cpython-3.16.0a1+freethreaded-macos-aarch64-none    <download available>
cpython-3.15.2-macos-aarch64-none                   /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.15 -> ../Cellar/python@3.15/3.15.2/bin/python3.15
cpython-3.15.2-macos-aarch64-none                   /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 -> ../Cellar/python@3.15/3.15.2/bin/python3
cpython-3.15.2-macos-aarch64-none                   <download available>
cpython-3.15.2+freethreaded-macos-aarch64-none      <download available>
cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none                  /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14 -> ../Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.10/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none                  <download available>
cpython-3.9.6-macos-aarch64-none                    /usr/bin/python3
pypy-3.12.15-macos-aarch64-none                     <download available>
graalpy-3.13.0-macos-aarch64-none                   <download available>
```

(shortened; your own list will be longer)

This is a **catalog, not an inventory**.
It is not a list of the Python versions you have installed.
It is a list of the versions `uv` can give you,
and on a new computer nearly every line will say `<download available>`,
meaning that version is *not* on your machine
and `uv` is offering to download it.

:::{.callout-note title="One installation can appear on several lines"}
`uv` lists every *path* that leads to a Python,
not every copy of Python.
One installation reached by two names is two lines.
This surprises people who have installed Python
through Homebrew or python.org before.

Here is a real example, filtered to just the 3.14 entries:

```bash
uv python list | grep 3.14
```

```out
cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none                  /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14 -> ../Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.10/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none                  <download available>
cpython-3.14.10+freethreaded-macos-aarch64-none     <download available>
cpython-3.14.3-macos-aarch64-none                   /Users/dan/.local/bin/python3.14 -> /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.14.3-macos-aarch64-none                   /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14
```

Five lines, but only **two** Pythons are installed:

- Line 1 is Homebrew's Python 3.14.10.
- Lines 2 and 3 are not installed at all.
  `uv` is offering to download its own 3.14.10,
  which is a different build than Homebrew's
  even though the version number matches,
  and a free-threaded build of it.
- Lines 4 and 5 are the *same* `uv`-managed installation,
  first the shortcut in `~/.local/bin`,
  then the real file in `~/.local/share/uv/python/` that it points to.
  The `->` shows a symlink.

Homebrew can do the same.
In the full list above,
its Python 3.15.2 appears twice,
as `python3.15` and as `python3`,
both pointing into the same folder.

Anything under `~/.local/share/uv/python/` is a Python that `uv` installed
and that `uv` manages.
That is where the Pythons for your projects will live.
:::

There are two columns.
The left is the version's full name,
and the right is either where it lives on your computer
or `<download available>`.

The name is made of five parts separated by dashes,
as in `cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none`:

- the **implementation**, `cpython`,
  which is the standard Python that almost everyone means by "Python".
  You will also see `pypy` and `graalpy`,
  which are alternative implementations.
  You do not need them.
- the **version**, `3.14.10`
- the **operating system**, `macos`
- the **architecture**, `aarch64` for Apple silicon,
  or `x86_64` for Intel machines
- the **libc**, which is `none` on macOS,
  and `gnu` or `musl` on Linux

A `+freethreaded` in the name,
such as `cpython-3.14.10+freethreaded-macos-aarch64-none`,
marks a special build of Python that runs without
the GIL (global interpreter lock).
You can ignore it for the projects in this book.

If what you actually want to ask
is "which Pythons do I have?",
there is a flag for that:

```bash
uv python list --only-installed
```

Example output:

```out
cpython-3.15.2-macos-aarch64-none     /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.15 -> ../Cellar/python@3.15/3.15.2/bin/python3.15
cpython-3.15.2-macos-aarch64-none     /opt/homebrew/bin/python3 -> ../Cellar/python@3.15/3.15.2/bin/python3
cpython-3.14.10-macos-aarch64-none    /opt/homebrew/bin/python3.14 -> ../Cellar/python@3.14/3.14.10/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.14.3-macos-aarch64-none     /Users/dan/.local/bin/python3.14 -> /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.14.3-macos-aarch64-none     /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.14-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.14
cpython-3.13.12-macos-aarch64-none    /Users/dan/.local/bin/python3.13 -> /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13
cpython-3.13.12-macos-aarch64-none    /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13
cpython-3.13.0-macos-aarch64-none     /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.13.0-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.13
cpython-3.12.13-macos-aarch64-none    /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.12
cpython-3.12.7-macos-aarch64-none     /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.12.7-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.12
cpython-3.11.16-macos-aarch64-none    /Users/dan/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.11-macos-aarch64-none/bin/python3.11
cpython-3.9.6-macos-aarch64-none      /usr/bin/python3
```

:::{.callout-warning title="Do not use system Python"}
Depending on your operating system and computer,
Python may be installed by default (e.g., `/usr/bin/python3`).
This is the system Python.
This is the Python that your operating system uses for its own tools.
Do not use or change this version of Python,
because you can break operating system tools that depend on it.
This is another reason why virtual environments are important.
:::

To install a specific version:

```bash
uv python install 3.14
```

You will rarely run that command directly.
More often you will pin a version for a project,
and `uv` will download it for you the first time it needs it.
You will see how in [uv: projects](0530-virtual-environments-python-uv-projects.qmd).
